claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy without a significant dedicated alumina-forming element is susceptible to rapid high-temperature oxidation.
Adding approximately 5 at.% aluminum to the base alloy will enable in situ formation of a protective alumina layer.
Aluminum addition will promote rapid formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 scale at high temperature.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be adherent.
The Al2O3 scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen and metal ions.
Aluminum in the alloy oxidizes preferentially at high temperatures to form Al2O3.
Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and has low oxygen-ion permeability.
A continuous alumina layer limits further oxygen ingress and oxidation of the underlying metals.
The aluminum-enhanced alloy will have better oxidation resistance than the untreated alloy during prolonged extreme-temperature exposure.
At 1100 °C in air or an oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours, the aluminum-enhanced alloy will show approximately 20–30% lower weight gain than the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy will form less protective oxides and consequently exhibit higher weight gain and more extensive oxidation under the same conditions.
The proposed benefit depends on the alloy system supporting formation of a coherent and continuous alumina scale.
Insufficient aluminum solubility or an inhomogeneous aluminum distribution may prevent formation of a protective alumina scale.
Competing oxide-forming elements may undermine formation of a pure Al2O3 layer.
The aluminum concentration needed to balance mechanical properties and oxidation resistance depends on alloy composition and processing history.
